content: Bacteremia, also referred to as bacteraemia in British English, is the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream. It is sometimes colloquially called blood poisoning or toxemia. Unlike sepsis, which involves the replication and systemic effects of pathogens, bacteremia specifically refers to the mere presence of bacteria in the blood without necessarily indicating active infection or replication. Diagnosis Bacteremia is most commonly diagnosed through blood cultures. In this process, a sample of blood is incubated with a medium that promotes bacterial growth. Since blood is normally sterile, the growth of bacteria in this medium indicates their presence in the bloodstream. If bacteria are present in the blood at the time the sample is collected, they will multiply in the culture medium, allowing for detection. However, bacteria that accidentally contaminate the culture medium during the collection process can also grow, which is why strict sterile techniques are essential when drawing blood for culture. Occasionally, blood cultures may reveal bacteria that originate from contamination of the skin through which the sample was obtained. To distinguish between transient and persistent bacteremia, blood cultures should be repeated at intervals. Excluding Endocarditis A clinical prediction rule is used to identify patients with bacteremia caused by Staphylococcus aureus who may be at risk of developing bacterial endocarditis, a serious infection of the heart valves. Causes In hospital settings, indwelling catheters are a common cause of bacteremia and subsequent nosocomial infections. These devices provide a pathway for bacteria, typically found on the skin, to enter the bloodstream. Other causes of bacteremia include dental procedures (even simple activities like tooth brushing), herpes infections (including herpetic whitlow), urinary tract infections, intravenous drug use, and colorectal cancer. Bacteremia can also occur during or after surgeries or explorations involving the oropharyngeal, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary systems. Certain drugs, such as caspofungin acetate and indinavir, have also been associated with bacteremia. Consequences Bacteremia serves as a primary mechanism for the spread of localized infections to distant organs, a process known as hematogenous dissemination. This is a key factor in the pathophysiology of conditions such as meningitis, endocarditis, aortitis, Pott's disease, and various forms of osteomyelitis. While bacteremia is typically transient due to the immune system's robust response, it can lead to more severe conditions. Septicemia, a related condition, involves the presence of bacteria or their toxins in the bloodstream and often triggers a systemic immune response. This response, characterized by symptoms such as fever, chills, and hypotension, is referred to as sepsis. In cases of more severe systemic disturbances, such as abnormalities in temperature, respiration, heart rate, or white blood cell count, the condition may progress to sepsis syndrome, septic shock, or even multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. Follow-Up In certain clinical scenarios, follow-up blood cultures are necessary to confirm the resolution of bacteremia. These scenarios include infections caused by gram-positive cocci (such as enterococci), the presence of a central venous catheter or endovascular source, hemodialysis, or persistent fever. Follow-up blood cultures may remain positive for the same pathogen in 7% to 14% of patients. If repeat blood cultures are obtained within the first 72 hours of initiating antibiotics, the positivity rate can be as high as 46%. Special techniques may be required when repeating blood cultures in patients with intravenous catheters to ensure accurate results.
